summary: Panama is visa-free for well over a hundred nationalities — including the whole EU, the UK, the US, Canada and most of Latin America — with tourist stays commonly set at 90 days. Everyone else needs either a stamped consular visa or, for a restricted list of nationalities, an authorized visa cleared in advance by the National Immigration Service; holders of a used US, Canadian, British, Australian or Schengen visa can often skip the visa entirely.

primarySources.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

defaultSource.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

conditionalWaivers.text: Travelers who would otherwise need a Panamanian visa can usually enter without one if they hold a valid visa or residence permit from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia or a Schengen country, provided it has already been used at least once to enter the issuing country and has several months of validity left. The stay granted is normally 30 days. Nationalities on Panama's authorized-visa list are excluded. Confirm with a Panamanian consulate or your airline before booking.

passportValidity.text: Panamanian law sets the minimum at 3 months' passport validity, but airlines routinely apply a 6-month rule and immigration officers prefer it — travel with at least 6 months to avoid being turned away at check-in.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required if you arrive from or have transited a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Vaccination is separately recommended — and sometimes checked — if you plan to travel to Darién or the eastern mainland provinces.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry condition, but private hospitals in Panama City expect payment or a guarantee up front, and evacuation from Bocas del Toro or Guna Yala is costly.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

onwardTicket.text: A confirmed onward or return ticket is a formal entry condition and is checked by airlines at check-in as well as at immigration. One-way arrivals are regularly refused boarding.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

proofOfFunds.text: Visitors are expected to show around USD 500 in cash, a recent bank statement or a credit card. Checks are not made on every arrival, but officers do ask, especially of travelers arriving overland or on one-way-looking itineraries.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

declarations.name: Customs declaration
declarations.text: A customs declaration is completed on arrival, covering goods, cash and agricultural products. Panama has run electronic versions at Tocumen at times — follow the instructions given on your flight.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

currencyLimits.text: Cash or bearer instruments of USD 10,000 or more must be declared on arrival and departure; undeclared amounts are seized.

source.name: Servicio Nacional de Migración de Panamá

notes: Fresh produce, meat, dairy and plants are restricted. Declare them or leave them behind.
Panama is a major transit country for narcotics and screening is intense; never carry a package for someone else.
Duty-free allowances are generous in Colón Free Zone purchases but receipts are checked on domestic onward flights.

currency.name: United States dollar (the balboa circulates only as coins, at par)

payments.text: Panama uses the US dollar, so there is no currency to change. Cards are accepted across Panama City, Boquete and resort areas; carry small notes for taxis, buses, Guna Yala and the islands, where cash is often the only option.

safety.text: Panama City, Boquete, Bocas del Toro and the canal corridor are comfortable for visitors, with opportunistic theft the main concern. The Darién Gap on the Colombian border is genuinely dangerous and should not be crossed overland; parts of Colón also warrant care.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Panama travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: The dry season from mid-December to April is the reliable window for the canal, the highlands and both coasts. May to November brings heavy afternoon rain, though it is quieter and cheaper.

tips.text: If you need a Panamanian visa, check whether you already hold a used US, Canadian, UK, Australian or Schengen visa — that alone usually lets you enter for 30 days without applying. Carry the original document, not a photocopy, and be ready to show the entry stamp proving it has been used.
Airlines enforce the onward-ticket rule at check-in more strictly for Panama than for most of the region. Book a refundable outbound flight or a bus ticket to Costa Rica before you fly.

There is no legal or safe overland route between Panama and Colombia. The Darién Gap is controlled by armed groups and smugglers — travel between the two countries by air or by a licensed boat service only.
Panama City's tap water is safe to drink, which is unusual in the region, but Bocas del Toro and some rural areas are exceptions. Use bottled or filtered water there.
The Guna Yala (San Blas) islands are autonomous territory: expect separate community entry fees payable in cash, and permission is needed for drones and some photography.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Panama?
faq.answer: For most travelers, no. Panama waives visas for well over a hundred nationalities, including all EU and Schengen states, the UK, Ireland, the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Israel and most of South and Central America — tourist stays are commonly granted for 90 days. Everyone else needs a stamped visa from a consulate, or an authorized visa cleared in advance if their nationality is on Panama's restricted list.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Panama as a tourist?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt visitors are normally admitted for 90 days, and some nationalities have historically been granted up to 180. The officer decides the number of days and writes it in the system, so check your stamp on arrival and apply to the Servicio Nacional de Migración for an extension before it runs out.

faq.question: Can I enter Panama with a US or Schengen visa instead of a Panamanian one?
faq.answer: Usually yes. If you hold a valid visa or residence permit from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia or a Schengen country that you have already used at least once to enter that country, Panama normally admits you for 30 days without a Panamanian visa. Nationalities on the authorized-visa list are excluded, and airlines apply the rule strictly. Confirm with a Panamanian consulate before booking.

faq.question: What is the difference between a stamped visa and an authorized visa?
faq.answer: A stamped visa (visa estampada) is decided by the Panamanian consulate itself and takes a week or two. An authorized visa (visa autorizada) applies to a restricted list of nationalities and must first be approved by the National Immigration Service in Panama, usually with a sponsor in the country. Allow one to three months.

faq.question: Do I need to show money to enter Panama?
faq.answer: Officially yes — around USD 500 in cash, a bank statement or a credit card, alongside a confirmed onward ticket. It is not requested on every arrival, but it is asked for often enough that you should have something ready, particularly if you are arriving overland.

faq.question: What currency does Panama use?
faq.answer: The US dollar is legal tender and used for all notes; the balboa exists only as coins, pegged one to one. There is nothing to exchange if you arrive with dollars, and ATMs dispense USD.
